{{< include ../_extensions/r-wasm/live/_knitr.qmd >}}

These exercises practise ANOVA, linear regression, and logistic regression on Elaf's data. Where you see `______`, replace it with your own code.

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: [ex1, ex2, ex3, ex4, ex5, ex6]
library(dplyr)
students      <- read.csv("students.csv")
semesters     <- read.csv("semesters.csv")
questionnaire <- read.csv("questionnaire.csv")
scores <- questionnaire |>
  mutate(
    stress_4 = 6 - stress_4,
    stress   = rowMeans(pick(stress_1:stress_6), na.rm = TRUE),
    support  = rowMeans(pick(support_1:support_6), na.rm = TRUE),
    burnout  = rowMeans(pick(burnout_1:burnout_6), na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  select(student_id, stress, support, burnout)
study <- students |>
  left_join(scores, join_by(student_id)) |>
  left_join(semesters |> filter(semester == 1), join_by(student_id))
```

## ANOVA

### Exercise 1: Wellbeing across faculties

Does first-semester wellbeing differ between faculties? Run a one-way ANOVA and calculate $\eta^2$. Should you run Tukey's test?

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex1
wellbeing_anova <- aov(wellbeing ~ ______, data = study)
summary(wellbeing_anova)
ss <- summary(wellbeing_anova)[[1]][["Sum Sq"]]
ss[1] / sum(ss)
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex1" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
wellbeing_anova <- aov(wellbeing ~ faculty, data = study)
summary(wellbeing_anova)
ss <- summary(wellbeing_anova)[[1]][["Sum Sq"]]
ss[1] / sum(ss)
```

The p-value is about 0.09, above 0.05, and $\eta^2$ is about 0.01: no evidence that wellbeing differs between faculties. Post-hoc tests are run only after a significant ANOVA, so there is no need for Tukey's test here. (Stress did differ between faculties; wellbeing does not.)
:::
:::

## Linear regression

### Exercise 2: One predictor

Regress first-semester wellbeing on sleep hours. Interpret the slope and R-squared.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex2
wb_simple <- lm(______ ~ sleep_hours, data = study)
summary(wb_simple)
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex2" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
wb_simple <- lm(wellbeing ~ sleep_hours, data = study)
summary(wb_simple)
```

Each extra hour of sleep goes with wellbeing about 5.3 points higher, and sleep alone explains about 21% of the differences in wellbeing.
:::
:::

### Exercise 3: More predictors

Add stress and support to the model. What happens to the slope of sleep, and to R-squared?

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex3
wb_multiple <- lm(wellbeing ~ sleep_hours + ______ + ______, data = study)
summary(wb_multiple)
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex3" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
wb_multiple <- lm(wellbeing ~ sleep_hours + stress + support, data = study)
summary(wb_multiple)
```

The slope of sleep drops from about 5.3 to about 3.9: part of what looked like the effect of sleep was really stress, because stressed students also sleep less. R-squared doubles, to about 0.43. Each point of stress lowers wellbeing by about 6 points, holding sleep and support constant.
:::
:::

### Exercise 4: A categorical predictor

Add `study_mode` to the model from Exercise 3. What is the reference category, and what does the coefficient mean?

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex4
wb_mode <- lm(wellbeing ~ sleep_hours + stress + support + ______, data = study)
summary(wb_mode)$coefficients
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex4" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
wb_mode <- lm(wellbeing ~ sleep_hours + stress + support + study_mode, data = study)
summary(wb_mode)$coefficients
```

The reference category is `Full-time` (first in alphabetical order), so the coefficient `study_modePart-time` compares part-time with full-time students. Part-time students' wellbeing is about 3 points lower, holding sleep, stress, and support constant, and the difference is significant.
:::
:::

## Logistic regression

### Exercise 5: Burnout and dropout

Fit a logistic regression of considering dropout on burnout, and turn the coefficient into an odds ratio with a confidence interval.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex5
study <- study |> mutate(dropout = as.integer(considering_dropout == "Yes"))
burnout_model <- glm(dropout ~ burnout, data = study, family = ______)
exp(cbind(coef(burnout_model), confint.default(burnout_model)))
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex5" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
study <- study |> mutate(dropout = as.integer(considering_dropout == "Yes"))
burnout_model <- glm(dropout ~ burnout, data = study, family = binomial)
exp(cbind(coef(burnout_model), confint.default(burnout_model)))
```

The odds ratio for burnout is about 3.7 (95% CI about 2.5 to 5.4): each extra point of burnout multiplies the odds of considering dropout by nearly four.
:::
:::

### Exercise 6: A predicted probability

Using the model from Exercise 5, what is the predicted probability of considering dropout for a student with a burnout score of 2, and for one with a score of 4?

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex6
study <- study |> mutate(dropout = as.integer(considering_dropout == "Yes"))
burnout_model <- glm(dropout ~ burnout, data = study, family = binomial)
predict(burnout_model, newdata = data.frame(burnout = c(2, 4)), type = ______)
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex6" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
predict(burnout_model, newdata = data.frame(burnout = c(2, 4)), type = "response")
```

`type = "response"` gives probabilities. A student with low burnout has only a small chance of considering dropout; one with high burnout, a much larger chance.
:::
:::
